strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: reducing expensive simulator calls for Bayesian inference using cheaper, domain-informed models.
The core method is simple and compatible with existing neural posterior estimation pipelines. Dummy parameters provide a straightforward way to accommodate differing parameter spaces.

Experiments demonstrate improvements over NPE across an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck benchmark and two neuroscience simulators, including a 24-parameter spiking network. Table 1 reports a useful improvement in plausible network outputs from 66.4% to 95.6%.

Evaluation includes reference-posterior comparisons, held-out log scores, posterior predictive checks, and some simulation-based calibration. Low-fidelity dataset sizes and multiple network initializations are explored.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: MF-NPE applies conventional pretraining and full fine-tuning to an existing density estimator, while MF-TSNPE adds this initialization to an existing sequential method. The paper offers little analysis of when transfer helps, fails, or introduces negative transfer, beyond selected favorable simulator pairs.

Comparisons are insufficient to establish competitiveness. In particular, MF-TSNPE is compared with amortized NPE without a standard TSNPE baseline, confounding transfer benefits with observation-specific sequential sampling. No existing multifidelity inference approach or alternative strategy for combining low- and high-fidelity data is evaluated.

High-fidelity sample savings do not establish total computational savings. In the neuron experiment, low-fidelity simulations are only seven times cheaper: 100,000 low-fidelity simulations alone cost roughly 14,300 high-fidelity equivalents. Accuracy-versus-total-cost comparisons should include simulation, pretraining, fine-tuning, and ensemble costs, with any reuse assumptions stated explicitly.

The active-learning extension knowingly omits proposal correction despite selecting 20% of each round through acquisition. Uncorrected conditional likelihood training generally targets the posterior induced by the altered sampling distribution. Minor C2ST gains on OU2 do not establish that the resulting bias is acceptable; calibration and acquisition-fraction sensitivity are missing.

Evidence for generality and posterior reliability remains limited. Transfer gains become small in OU3/OU4, sequential variants are demonstrated only on OU2, and the 24-parameter application lacks calibration diagnostics. Its broad firing-rate acceptance criterion measures practical plausibility rather than agreement with the observation-conditioned posterior. Repeated training on fixed simulation datasets also does not measure variability across independently generated datasets.

The reference-posterior benchmark needs clarification. Appendix B generates OU trajectories using Euler–Maruyama but constructs reference posteriors using the exact continuous-time transition likelihood, without reporting a discretization-error check. It is also unclear whether the reference likelihood conditions on exactly the same ten subsampled observations provided to the estimator.

Reproducibility is incomplete: optimizer settings, learning rates, batch sizes, stopping criteria, and an accessible code link are absent. There are consequential specification inconsistencies, including 14 versus 24 high-fidelity parameters and a neuron stimulus described as 0.3 nA in the main text versus 0.55 mV in Appendix C.

strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck in simulation-based inference: reducing expensive simulator calls by exploiting cheaper approximations. The basic pretraining and fine-tuning procedure is simple and readily applicable.
Reports consistent improvements over NPE at small high-fidelity budgets across an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck benchmark and two neuroscience simulators, including a 24-parameter application.

Evaluation includes reference-posterior C2ST, held-out log scores, and single-neuron calibration and posterior predictive checks. Table 1 reports improved generation of plausible network activity, from 66.4% for NPE to 95.6% for MF-NPE.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: MF-NPE applies standard pretraining and unrestricted fine-tuning to an existing posterior estimator, MF-TSNPE adds existing truncated sequential inference, and the acquisition rule is borrowed from prior work. There is no substantial analysis explaining when transfer helps or fails.

Comparisons are insufficient to establish the sequential contribution. Figure 3 lacks a standard TSNPE baseline, so improvements over amortized NPE cannot isolate the benefit of multifidelity transfer from sequential simulation allocation. The sequential variants are demonstrated only on OU2, and no existing multifidelity inference method is compared experimentally.

A-MF-TSNPE deliberately uses an uncorrected acquisition-biased proposal while retaining the ordinary posterior-estimation loss. Appendix F.2 selects 20% of samples this way, which changes the training target in general. Small C2ST improvements on OU2 do not establish that the resulting posterior bias or coverage errors are acceptable; acquisition-fraction ablations and calibration tests are missing.

High-fidelity sample savings do not establish overall computational savings. In the neuron experiment, low-fidelity simulation is only approximately seven times cheaper, making 100,000 low-fidelity samples equivalent to roughly 14,300 high-fidelity calls before training overhead. Cost-matched comparisons and end-to-end runtimes are needed to substantiate the computational-efficiency claims.

The evaluation does not systematically vary fidelity mismatch or test negative transfer. OU gains become small as additional parameters are introduced. The 24-parameter application uses only two firing-rate summaries and lacks posterior calibration; meeting broad firing-rate bounds demonstrates plausibility rather than accurate posterior recovery.

Reproducibility and reference validation need improvement. Optimizer settings, learning rates, and concrete stopping criteria are unspecified. The neuron stimulus differs between Section 4.2 and Appendix C. The OU simulator uses Euler–Maruyama, whereas reference inference uses an exact continuous-time transition likelihood; discretization error and consistency with the subsampled observations are not checked. Repeated network initializations on fixed simulation datasets also omit variation across independently generated training datasets.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck: posterior inference when accurate scientific simulators are expensive. Low-fidelity pretraining followed by high-fidelity fine-tuning is simple, useful, and compatible with existing NPE implementations.

The experiments demonstrate improved high-fidelity sample efficiency across three tasks, including two substantive neuroscience simulators. In the spiking-network experiment, the fraction of posterior samples producing plausible firing rates increases from 66.4% to 95.6%.

The evaluation includes complementary diagnostics: reference-posterior C2ST for the OU task, held-out NLTP, posterior predictive checks, and simulation-based calibration for the neuron model. Multiple network initializations and low-fidelity dataset sizes provide useful supporting evidence.
Padding low-fidelity parameter spaces with prior-distributed dummy variables provides a practical way to transfer between simulators with different parameter dimensionalities.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. The principal method applies standard pretraining and unrestricted fine-tuning to an existing posterior estimator; its extensions combine this with established TSNPE and ensemble-variance acquisition. The paper lacks a deeper analysis or sufficiently comprehensive empirical study to establish a strong contribution beyond this straightforward combination.

The comparisons do not isolate the sequential contribution. Figure 3 compares MF-TSNPE against amortized NPE and MF-NPE without a standard TSNPE baseline. Consequently, the gains cannot be attributed specifically to multifidelity transfer rather than observation-specific sequential sampling. Comparisons with alternative multifidelity inference approaches are also absent.

The computational-efficiency claim is not established through matched total-cost comparisons. Experiments primarily count high-fidelity simulations while excluding low-fidelity generation and pretraining. For the neuron model, low-fidelity simulations are only approximately seven times cheaper, so 100,000 low-fidelity simulations cost roughly 14,300 high-fidelity simulations before fine-tuning. Fewer high-fidelity calls therefore need not imply lower overall cost.

A-MF-TSNPE deliberately omits correction for its non-prior acquisition distribution. Appendix F.2 selects 20% of each round through acquisition, which can introduce systematic posterior bias under the uncorrected likelihood objective. Small C2ST improvements on OU2 do not establish that this tradeoff preserves calibration; bias and acquisition-fraction ablations are needed.

The empirical scope does not adequately characterize when transfer succeeds or fails. There is no controlled fidelity-mismatch study or negative-transfer analysis, and improvements become small in OU4. The largest parameter-space experiment uses only two firing-rate summaries and lacks posterior calibration diagnostics; plausible firing rates alone do not establish accurate posterior uncertainty.

The reference-posterior evaluation needs clarification. Appendix B generates OU trajectories with Euler–Maruyama but constructs reference posteriors using the exact continuous-time transition likelihood. The discretization error and consistency of the reference likelihood with the ten retained observations are not established.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful architecture and prior details. Optimizer settings, learning rates, stopping settings, and acquisition-pool size are unspecified. There are also conflicting descriptions of the spiking model dimensionality and injected current. Repeated initializations use fixed simulation datasets, so the reported intervals do not capture variability across independently generated training datasets.

strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck in simulation-based inference through a simple, implementable strategy: low-fidelity pretraining followed by high-fidelity fine-tuning.
The evaluation spans statistical benchmarks, image observations, and two neuroscience applications, including a 24-parameter spiking network with genuinely expensive simulations.

Results provide evidence that pretraining improves low-budget inference over NPE and TSNPE. Supporting experiments examine low-fidelity dataset size, differing parameter dimensions, alternative pretraining, and representation perturbations.

The manuscript provides architectural details, repeated initializations, posterior predictive checks, some calibration diagnostics, and computational cost measurements rather than relying exclusively on simulation counts.
weaknesses: The active extension has an unresolved statistical correctness issue. Appendix M.2 explicitly acknowledges that acquisition-selected parameters bias the proposal, yet Algorithm 4 trains with an uncorrected posterior-estimation loss. Its population target therefore generally differs from the desired posterior. Selecting 20% of samples actively does not establish negligible bias, and calibration results for ordinary MF-NPE do not validate A-MF-TSNPE. A corrected objective or convincing bias and coverage analysis is needed.

The SIR multifidelity benchmark appears degenerate as specified in Appendix E.5. Both fidelities use identical equations for S and I, identical initial conditions, and observations derived only from I. Removing the R equation cannot change those observations because R does not feed back into their dynamics. Consequently, this experiment does not establish transfer between distinct simulator fidelities; any implemented difference must be specified and reconciled with the reported posterior discrepancies.

The methodological novelty is limited: the core algorithm is standard full-network fine-tuning, its sequential version builds directly on TSNPE, and the acquisition criterion is established ensemble variance. Comparisons primarily against training from scratch and MF-ABC do not sufficiently establish an advance over alternative neural multifidelity or transfer strategies. Concurrent related methods are cited but receive little substantive comparison.

The strongest efficiency claims are not established at matched posterior accuracy. Appendix K compares L5PC NPE at NLTP -5.87 with A-MF-TSNPE at -5.08, and spiking-network NPE at -4.72 with MF-NPE at -4.08; lower is better. These differences exceed the reported uncertainties. The timing results demonstrate useful tradeoffs, but do not substantiate the quoted speedups at equivalent accuracy, particularly for the active method.

Posterior validation is incomplete where it matters most. Calibration is shown for amortized inference on the two-parameter neuron task at one high-fidelity budget, but not for the active extension or the 24-parameter application. Firing-rate success and NRMSE cannot establish calibrated uncertainty. The OU reference also uses an exact continuous-time likelihood despite Euler–Maruyama simulation; discretization effects and alignment with the subsampled observations should be verified.

Reproducibility is weakened by inconsistent experimental descriptions and unavailable review-time code. Evaluation counts differ between the main text and Appendix D.1, while the neuron stimulus is described as a noisy 0.3 nA current in Section 4.2 and a 0.55 mV step in Appendix G. These discrepancies are consequential given the benchmark and sampling concerns.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: reducing expensive simulations for Bayesian inference. Low-fidelity pretraining followed by high-fidelity fine-tuning is simple and compatible with existing neural posterior estimators.

The empirical study spans four benchmark tasks and two neuroscience applications, including a 24-parameter spiking network. Several experiments show substantial improvements over training from scratch at small high-fidelity budgets.

Provides multiple evaluation metrics, repeated network initializations, posterior predictive checks, some calibration diagnostics, and explicit computational-cost measurements. Experiments also examine differing parameter dimensions and alternative pretraining strategies.
weaknesses: The active-learning variant has an unresolved posterior-correctness problem. Algorithm 4 mixes variance-selected parameters with truncated-prior samples but trains with an uncorrected likelihood loss. Its population target is therefore proportional to the acquisition-induced sampling distribution times the likelihood, rather than the desired prior times likelihood. Appendix M.2 acknowledges this bias, but choosing a 20% acquisition fraction neither bounds nor removes it. Calibration tests for the active variant and acquisition-fraction ablations are missing.

The SIR multifidelity benchmark is questionable as specified in Appendix E.5. Both fidelities use identical equations for S and I, identical initial conditions, and observations derived only from I. Removing the R equation does not change these dynamics because R never feeds back into them. Thus, the stated models produce the same observations, making this effectively additional same-model training data rather than evidence of transfer across fidelities. Any implemented difference needs to be documented.

Methodological novelty is limited: the central method is standard pretraining and full-network fine-tuning, extended to TSNPE with an existing ensemble-variance acquisition rule. The paper cites closely related neural multifidelity and active SBI methods but does not compare against them. Comparisons primarily against NPE, TSNPE, and MF-ABC do not sufficiently establish competitiveness or isolate acquisition benefits from ensemble benefits.

The strongest efficiency claims are not consistently demonstrated at matched accuracy. Appendix K reports spiking-network NLTP of -4.72 ± 0.01 for NPE versus -4.08 ± 0.01 for MF-NPE, and neuron-model NLTP of -5.87 ± 0.04 for NPE versus -5.08 ± 0.27 for the active variant; lower is better. These differences require justification before the associated cost reductions can be described as preserving accuracy. Total-cost-versus-accuracy curves would be more convincing than selected operating points.

The analysis of when transfer helps overstates its evidence. Appendix B studies one controlled OU setting, yet concludes that mutual information is necessary for effective transfer and depicts a performance bound without deriving one. Appendix C only establishes the standard population NPE loss identity, not transfer-learning convergence rates or correctness of the active algorithm.

Reproducibility is weakened by inconsistent experimental descriptions: the neuron stimulus differs between Section 4.2 and Appendix G, and evaluation sample counts differ between the main text, figure captions, and Appendix D.1. Code and data are promised only upon publication, limiting the ability to resolve these discrepancies.

strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck: reducing expensive simulations while retaining useful Bayesian parameter inference. The basic low-fidelity pretraining followed by high-fidelity fine-tuning approach is simple and readily compatible with existing NPE workflows.

The evaluation spans four benchmark tasks and two neuroscience applications, including a 24-parameter spiking network. Handling parameters absent from the low-fidelity model through dummy variables is a useful practical feature.

The neuroscience experiments provide encouraging evidence of improved simulation efficiency, supported by posterior predictive checks, calibration results for amortized inference, and explicit simulation and training cost measurements.
The appendices provide substantial implementation detail and investigate pretraining budgets, differing parameter dimensions, alternative pretraining datasets, and controlled simulator perturbations.
weaknesses: The active extension has an unresolved correctness problem. Appendix M.2 explicitly acknowledges that acquisition-selected parameters bias the proposal, yet Algorithm 4 uses an uncorrected NPE loss. Its population target therefore generally differs from the desired posterior. Fixing the active fraction at 20% does not establish negligible bias, and the reported calibration checks do not validate this extension. A corrected objective or convincing bias and coverage analysis is needed.

The SIR multifidelity benchmark appears degenerate as specified in Appendix E.5. Both fidelities use identical equations for S and I, identical initial conditions, and observations derived only from I; removing the R equation does not change these dynamics because R does not feed back into them. Thus, the stated setup does not establish distinct observation distributions across fidelities. This undermines one benchmark and requires reconciliation with the reported posterior differences.

Methodological novelty is limited: the core method applies standard pretraining and full-network fine-tuning to NPE, then incorporates existing TSNPE and ensemble-variance acquisition machinery. The paper cites closely related transfer-learning and multifidelity SBI work but does not experimentally establish its advantages over those approaches. Appendix C establishes the standard population NPE objective identity, rather than a transfer-learning efficiency result.

The strongest computational savings are not demonstrated at clearly matched accuracy. In Table 5, the L5PC comparison gives NLTP -5.87 for NPE versus -5.08 for A-MF-TSNPE, and the network comparison gives -4.72 versus -4.08 for MF-NPE, with lower values preferable. These results support a cost–accuracy tradeoff, but do not by themselves establish equivalent-quality speedups. Comparing amortized NPE with observation-specific sequential inference also requires accounting for the number of observations analyzed.

The acquisition contribution is insufficiently isolated. It improves the OU task but not significantly SLCP or SIR, and lacks a matched ensemble baseline without acquisition to separate sample-selection benefits from ensembling. An active-fraction ablation and calibration measurements would be particularly important given the acknowledged bias.

Reproducibility is weakened by inconsistencies in experimental descriptions: evaluation counts differ between the main text and Appendix D.1, and the neuron stimulus is described as a noisy 0.3 nA current in Section 4.2 but a 0.55 mV step in Appendix G. Code and data are promised only upon publication, leaving these discrepancies unresolved in the submitted evidence.
